name: Social Media and Media Consent
title: Social Media and Media Consent
answer: Schools can use AI to draft social media posts and design graphics, but every student photo shared publicly must first be checked against family consent. Some families opt out for safety reasons such as custody disputes or protective orders, and a mistake can put a child at risk. AI also makes posted images easier to take and alter into harmful fakes, so schools should limit how many student photos they post and where.

sections.body: This idea covers how schools handle social media and student images when AI tools make posting faster and easier. AI can draft posts and design graphics, and scheduling tools can plan content ahead, which saves time for the staff who manage communications. The content still needs to reflect the school's real life and voice rather than feeling generic. The deeper problem is consent and safety: photos of students require family permission before they appear in a post, newsletter, or website. Some families opt out for safety reasons, including custody disputes or protective orders, so a single unchecked photo can put a child at risk.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day school communications, staff may use AI to draft social media posts and create graphics, then schedule them in advance. Before anything with a student's image goes out, whether in a post, a newsletter, or on the website, the school confirms that the family has given permission. The book does not give grade band variations for this practice. Schools are also asked to think carefully about how many student photos they post and where those photos appear. The text notes that the content should reflect the school's real life and voice, so AI drafting is a starting point rather than the final word.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It describes practice and risk rather than research findings. The one legal reference it makes is to Chapter 3, which described the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which makes sharing intimate deepfakes a crime. That reference is used to explain why schools should think carefully about how many student photos they post and where. Otherwise, the guidance rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Consent is the central limit: before any student's photo appears in a post, newsletter, or website, the school must confirm that the family has given permission. Some families opt out for safety reasons, including custody disputes or protective orders, and a mistake here can put a child at risk. AI raises new concerns because photos posted online can be taken and altered, including into harmful fakes. The text points to the TAKE IT DOWN Act, which makes sharing intimate deepfakes a crime. The decisions about how many student photos to post and where stay with the school and the people responsible for communications, not with the AI tools.
